stories.title: The amazing disappearing exoplanet
stories.summary: An exoplanet seems to have stopped transiting in front of its host star.

stories.title: White dwarf star glows an eerie green
stories.summary: Pink, purple and blue white dwarfs also exist, upending common ideas about these end-of-life stellar remnants

stories.title: Optical experiment demonstrates the strong Mpemba effect in a single qubit
stories.summary: Researchers used an optical experiment to show a strong version of the Mpemba effect, in which a system that starts further from equilibrium can settle faster, in a single qubit, the basic unit of quantum information. The work explores how a disturbed system relaxes back to thermal equilibrium, the state with no net heat flow to its surroundings. This could help explain how quantum systems exchange energy with their environment.

stories.title: IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos
stories.summary: The IceCube observatory, a huge detector buried deep in Antarctic ice, is recording neutrinos from distant cosmic sources with energies roughly 10 billion times greater than those of neutrinos made by fusion in the Sun. Because neutrinos rarely interact with matter, they pass through our bodies and cross space almost undisturbed. Studying these energetic particles could reveal details of violent cosmic events and the early universe.

stories.title: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
stories.summary: Researchers propose that a type of neutrino, long neglected by physicists, may explain why matter outlasted antimatter after the Big Bang, which allowed stars, planets and life to form. The idea is that this particle changed conditions in the very early universe. If so, it may have left gravitational wave signals that future observations could detect, offering a way to test the proposal.

stories.title: Organisation Release: Ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula lurks within sight of Hubble and Webb
stories.summary: Hubble and Webb have imaged a dusty pillar nicknamed the Cat's Head Nebula inside the Carina Nebula, about 7,500 light-years from Earth. In visible light the dust looks opaque, but Webb's infrared images see through much of it, exposing embedded young stars and warm dust. Ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars ionises and heats the pillar's edges, slowly evaporating gas and shaping where new stars can form.
